list.title: Gear
list.lead: The board is only half the story — the right gear matters just as much for safety and enjoyment.

evezo.title: Paddle
evezo.short: Drives the board – length, weight and material matter.
evezo.purpose: The paddle provides the drive: the blade's size and shape, and the shaft's length and stiffness, determine how much energy each stroke takes and how much it loads your shoulders over a long session.
evezo.buying: Pick an adjustable-length paddle if several people share it, or if you're still dialing in your own setup — 15–20 cm above your height is a good starting point. Carbon is lighter and stiffer (less tiring over distance) but pricier; an aluminium/plastic combo is plenty for starting out.

poraz.title: Leash
poraz.short: Tethers you to the board – but the type depends on the water.
poraz.purpose: The leash keeps the board from drifting away from you after a fall — it's your most important link to your surface flotation device.
poraz.buying: On flat water an ankle leash is enough; on rivers you need a quick-release waist leash (see below why). Match the length roughly to the board's length — a thicker cord takes more load but drags slightly more in the water.

mentomelleny.title: PFD
mentomelleny.short: Not a luxury – especially on rivers and in cold water.
mentomelleny.purpose: A personal flotation device (PFD) keeps you afloat even if you lose consciousness or get exhausted — that's the difference between an uncomfortable and a genuinely dangerous situation.
mentomelleny.buying: For SUP, a compact, belt-pack style is the most comfortable — it only needs to inflate/activate after a fall. Children and non-swimmers always need a conventional, continuously worn vest, not a belt-pack.

pumpa.title: Pump
pumpa.short: Not optional on an inflatable board – it's core kit.
pumpa.purpose: An inflatable (iSUP) board only reaches its final stiffness at the manufacturer's pressure (typically 12–15 PSI) — without it, the board flexes and handles poorly on the water.
pumpa.buying: A double-action hand pump is faster at low pressure, but you need to switch to single-action for the high-pressure finish; an electric pump is more convenient but needs a car or battery power source. Check that the pump's connector fits your board's valve.

safety.title: An underinflated board is unstable
safety.body: Pressure below the manufacturer's PSI increases the board's flex on the water — this hurts stability and glide, and in extreme cases can lead to cracking or injury. Watch the gauge while pumping, not just the stroke count.

szarazzsak.title: Dry bag
szarazzsak.short: For touring and cold conditions it protects your gear, not just your comfort.
szarazzsak.purpose: A dry bag keeps your phone, clothes and first-aid kit dry and buoyant even if you capsize.
szarazzsak.buying: A roll-top closure is the most reliable; size the litres to the length of your trip. A separate, smaller waterproof pouch for your phone/keys is handy even if you also carry a bigger dry bag.

safety.title: Keep first aid and a signal device reachable
safety.body: On a longer tour or unfamiliar water, don't strap your first-aid kit and a waterproof phone case to the bottom of the board — in an emergency, quick access matters, not just staying dry.

ules.title: Seat
ules.short: Turns the board into kayak mode for longer distances.
ules.purpose: A seat attachment lets the SUP board be used kayak-style with a double-bladed paddle — a more restful position for long distances or strong wind.
ules.buying: Check that your board has D-rings or a strap system to attach the seat — most all-round and touring boards are set up for it from the factory, race boards less often.

uszony.title: Fin
uszony.short: Tracking and glide depend on it.
uszony.purpose: The fin holds a straight line and reduces side-slip — its size and shape affect how manoeuvrable the board is versus how well it tracks.
uszony.buying: The mounting type (US Box or FCS) depends on your board — check before buying. For shallow water or rivers, a shorter, flexible, or removable fin is recommended so it doesn't catch on the riverbed.

taska.title: Bag
taska.short: Transport and storage – matters most for an inflatable board.
taska.purpose: A carry bag (usually backpack-style) protects an inflatable board from abrasion and UV exposure during transport and storage.
taska.buying: Check that the bag's size fits your folded board and its accessories (pump, paddle) — a padded backpack strap matters a lot if you're carrying it to the shore on foot.

advisor.title: You'll also need this
advisor.lead: The board alone isn't enough — start out safely with these.

leash.river: On rivers you need a quick-release waist leash — an ankle leash can snag in moving water.
leash.other: An ankle leash tethers you to the board so it doesn't drift away after a fall.

advisor.pfd: A PFD or buoyancy aid — especially important for beginners and on rivers.
advisor.pump: An inflatable board also needs a pump — most sets include one, but check the pressure range.
advisor.drybag: For touring, a dry bag protects your clothes and gear from moisture.
